questions.question: Which task is the bin packing problem?
options: Choose the heaviest subset of items that fits into a single container.
Pack the items so that every container is filled exactly to capacity.
Pack as many items as possible into a fixed number of containers.
Pack every item, within capacity, into as few containers as possible.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT allowed in a feasible bin packing solution?
options: Leaving some of a container's capacity unused at the very end
Filling one container exactly up to its full capacity
Putting part of an item in one container, the rest in another
Putting a single heavy item into a container on its own

questions.question: For a bin packing instance, a feasible packing using 5 containers has been found. What does it show about the minimum number of containers?
options: The minimum is at least 5.
The minimum is at most 5.
The minimum is exactly 5.
The minimum is below 5.

questions.question: Items have weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$, and every container has capacity $C$. Which expression is the total-weight bound on the minimum number of containers?
options: $\left\lfloor\sum_i w_i/C\right\rfloor$
$\left\lceil\sum_i w_i/C\right\rceil$
$\left\lfloor\sum_i w_i/C\right\rfloor+1$
$\left\lceil\max_i w_i/C\right\rceil$

questions.question: Items of weights 15, 30, 20, 35 and 10 must be packed into containers of capacity 50. Which list of container contents is a feasible packing?
Items of weights 9, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2 are packed into containers of capacity 12 as $\{9,3\}$, $\{8,4\}$, $\{6,5\}$, $\{3,2\}$. What is the minimum number of containers?
options: Exactly 3
Exactly 4
At most 3
At least 5

questions.question: Items have weights $w_i$, containers have capacity $C$, $S_j$ is the set of items placed in container $j$, and $|S_j|$ is the number of items in it. Which condition expresses the capacity of container $j$?
options: $\sum_{i\notin S_j} w_i\le C$
$\sum_{i\in S_j} w_i\le C$
$|S_j|\le C$
$\sum_{i\in S_j} w_i=C$

questions.question: For a bin packing instance, the total-weight bound equals 3. Must some feasible packing with 3 containers exist?
options: Yes; the bound is always attained by some packing.
No; the bound can lie strictly below the true minimum.
Yes, provided no item is heavier than the capacity.
No; the minimum is always strictly above the bound.

questions.question: Why is $\lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil$, with item weights $w_i$ and capacity $C$, never larger than the minimum number of containers?
options: $k$ containers hold at most $kC$, so $kC\ge\sum_i w_i$, and $k$ is whole.
An optimal packing fills every container exactly up to the capacity $C$.
Sorting the items by weight packs them into exactly that many containers.
Each item weighs at most $C$, so every item needs its own container.

questions.question: Items have weights $w_i$ and containers have capacity $C$. A packing rule returns a feasible packing. When is that packing certainly optimal?
options: When every container in it is filled to more than half of $C$
When the items were sorted by weight before packing
When its number of containers equals $\lceil\sum_i w_i/C\rceil$
When no single item can be moved into any other container

questions.question: Items arrive in the order 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, and containers have capacity 10. A rule puts each item into the most recently opened container if it fits, and otherwise opens a new container. How many containers does the rule use, and what is the minimum?
options: The rule uses 4; the minimum is 4
The rule uses 3; the minimum is 3
The rule uses 4; the minimum is 3
The rule uses 5; the minimum is 4

questions.question: For one bin packing instance, two packing rules give feasible packings with 6 and 5 containers, and the total-weight bound is 4. What is known about the minimum number of containers?
options: It is exactly 5, the size of the best packing found
It is exactly 4, the value of the total-weight bound
It is 4, 5 or 6, between the bound and both packings
It is 4 or 5, between the bound and the best packing

questions.question: Items of weights 8, 7, 6, 5 and 4 must be packed into containers of capacity 10. A student proposes 3 containers: 8 plus 2 units of the item of weight 5; 7 plus its other 3 units; and $\{6,4\}$. Which assessment is correct?
options: Valid: each container then holds exactly 10, so 3 is the true minimum.
Invalid, but another packing with 3 containers does exist here.
Invalid: the total-weight bound already shows that 4 are needed.
Invalid: the item of weight 5 is split, and the true minimum is 4.

questions.question: Items have weights $w_i$ and containers capacity $C$. For a packing using $k$ containers, call $kC-\sum_i w_i$ its unused capacity. How does minimizing unused capacity relate to minimizing the number of containers?
options: They select the same packings, since $\sum_i w_i$ is fixed by the instance.
Minimizing unused capacity may need more than the minimum number of containers.
The two goals agree only when all items happen to have equal weights $w_i$.
The two goals agree only when every container is filled exactly to $C$.

questions.question: In a bin packing instance with item weights $w_i$ and common capacity $C$, which change can never increase the minimum number of containers?
options: Adding one more item of any weight to the instance
Replacing one of the items by a heavier one
Raising the common capacity $C$ of all containers
Doubling every item weight $w_i$ in the instance

questions.question: A student claims: if no two containers of a feasible packing can be merged into one container without exceeding the capacity, then the packing uses the minimum number of containers. Which assessment is correct?
options: True: when no merge is possible, every container is already more than half full.
False: $\{6,4\},\{6,4\}$ with capacity 10 allows no merge, yet 3 are needed.
True: merging two containers is the only way to reduce the number used.
False: $\{6\},\{6\},\{4,4\}$ with capacity 10 allows no merge, but 2 suffice.
